[1] In 1829 a London doctor named Nathaniel Ward buried the chrysalis of a moth in damp soil at the bottom of a glass jar, and sealed the lid. He wanted to watch the adult insect emerge. The moth did hatch, but by then Ward had noticed something more interesting: a small fern and a few blades of grass had sprouted from the soil.

[2] Ward had tried for years to grow ferns in his garden, and every attempt had failed. The air in his part of London was thick with coal smoke, which choked delicate plants. Inside the jar, however, the fern thrived. Water evaporated from the soil, condensed on the glass, and trickles back down, so the plant never needed watering. The seal also kept the smoke out. Ward left the jar on a windowsill for nearly four years without opening it, and the fern stayed green the entire time.

[3] [A] Ward soon had a carpenter build larger versions: wooden boxes with glass walls and tight lids. [B] He then wondered whether the cases could protect plants on long sea voyages. [C] In 1833 he packed two cases with ferns and grasses and shipped them to Sydney, where nearly every plant arrived alive after months on deck. [D] The return trip went just as well.

[4] The invention reshaped the plant trade. Before Wards' cases, nurseries that ordered plants from abroad had expected to lose nearly all of them; afterward, most survived. Around 1850 the botanist Robert Fortune used the cases to carry thousands of tea plants from China to India, there they became the start of a vast tea industry. Rubber and banana plants later traveled the same way.

[5] At home, the cases had a gentler effect. Victorian families set glass cases of ferns in their parlors, and a craze of collecting ferns swept the country. Ward himself kept a case on his desk for the rest of his life.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "Around 1850 the botanist Robert Fortune used the cases to carry thousands of tea plants from China to India, there they became the start of a vast tea industry." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "India, there they"?
explanation: "There they became the start of a vast tea industry" is an independent clause, so joining it to the first clause with a comma alone is a comma splice. "Where" turns it into a relative clause describing India, which a comma can attach. A semicolon cannot introduce a dependent "where" clause, and the comma after "where" splits the clause from its own subject.

passage_title: The Mold That Drew a Railway
passage:
[1] Physarum polycephalum has no brain, no nerves, and no eyes. It is a slime mold, a single enormous cell that creeps across the forest floor as a bright yellow film, feeding on bacteria and fungal spores. Yet in the past few decades this organism has solved problems that would challenge a team of engineers.

[2] In 2000 the Japanese researcher Toshiyuki Nakagaki placed pieces of a slime mold throughout a small plastic maze. The pieces merged into a single cell who filled every corridor. He then set an oat flake, one of the mold's favorite foods at the entrance and another at the exit. Within hours, for example, the mold had withdrawn from the dead ends, leaving one thick tube along the shortest route between the two flakes.

[3] Ten years later, Nakagaki and his colleague Atsushi Tero tried something more ambitious. On a wet dish shaped like the region around Tokyo, they placed oat flakes in positions, matching thirty-six cities and towns. The mold started at the spot representing Tokyo itself. Because it avoids bright light, the researchers lit the areas that stood for mountains and lakes, which kept the mold off ground where rail lines would be hard to build. After about a day the mold had linked every flake with a web of tubes. When the team compared that web with the real rail network around Tokyo, they found the two remarkably alike in their efficiency and in how well they would survive a broken link.

[4] The mold's method is simple. It begins by spreading in all directions. Tubes that carry a strong flow of nutrients between food sources thickens; tubes that carry little thin out and eventually vanish. No part of the cell plans the network, it emerges from countless local adjustments.

[5] Engineers have taken note. Researchers have since written computer programs that copy the mold's rules, and they hope such programs could help design road systems, power grids, and communication networks that keep working when one connection fails.
prompt: In paragraph 4, in the sentence "No part of the cell plans the network, it emerges from countless local adjustments." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "network, it emerges"?
explanation: Two independent clauses are joined by a comma alone. A semicolon separates them correctly, and "instead" marks that the network arises in place of being planned. Putting "instead" after the comma leaves the splice in place, and moving it before the comma attaches it to the first clause and still leaves the splice.

passage:
[1] The summer I turned sixteen, my cousin Ifeoma found me a job at Benedek Press, a print shop two blocks from our apartment. I pictured myself running a copier and answering the phone. Likewise, Mr. Benedek led me past the copiers to a back room. There, a black iron press, older than my grandmother stood under a single lamp.

[2] He handed me a wooden tray divided in dozens of small compartments, each holding metal letters of one kind. "Every word you have ever read," he said, "was once built like this." For the first week I did nothing but set type I picked letters out of the tray one at a time and lined them up, upside down and backward, in a small metal holder. A single wedding invitation took me most of a morning.

[3] [A] My first proofs were a mess. [B] I had confused the lowercase b and d, which look identical when reversed, and a few letters printed so faint they were barely visible. [C] Mr. Benedek never corrected me himself. [D] He would circle each error in pencil, hand the proof back, and returning to his own work.

[4] By August I could set a line nearly as fast as I could write it, and my proofs came back with fewer circles. The work had changed how I read, too. On cereal boxes and street signs I started to notice the spaces between letters, and the way a heavy letter could crowd a light one. Mr. Benedek called this "seeing the white."

[5] On my last day he printed a card for me on the iron press. He did not say much when he handed it to me. It said only my name, in letters I had set myself. I still keep it in my desk drawer, the ink pressed so deep I can feel each letter with my thumb.
prompt: The writer is considering adding the following sentence after the last sentence of paragraph 2 ("A single wedding invitation took me most of a morning."): "Every letter had to go in upside down and backward." Should the writer make this addition?
choices: Yes, because it explains how the narrator came to confuse the b and the d in paragraph 3.
No, because it contradicts paragraph 2's description of how the narrator lined up the letters.
Yes, because it explains why the invitation described in the preceding sentence took so long to set.
No, because paragraph 2 has already said that the letters were lined up upside down and backward.
correct_answer: No, because paragraph 2 has already said that the letters were lined up upside down and backward.
explanation: The third sentence of paragraph 2 already says the narrator lined the letters up "upside down and backward," so the new sentence only repeats it. Because that detail is already present, the addition explains nothing new about the slow invitation or the b and d, which paragraph 3 explains on its own, and it agrees with paragraph 2 rather than contradicting it.

passage:
[1] Off the coast of Alaska's Aleutian Islands, two kinds of seafloor lie within a short boat ride of each other. Around some islands, forests of kelp rises from the rocks, their golden fronds reaching the surface and sheltering schools of fish. Around others, the bottom is nearly bare, covered with spiny purple sea urchins and little else.

[2] In 1971 a young ecologist named James Estes set out to learn why. He noticed that the islands with kelp forests had large numbers of sea otters, while the bare islands had almost none. Otters eat sea urchins, and sea urchins eat kelp. Where otters were plentiful, he reasoned they kept the urchins in check, and the kelp was free to grow. Where otters were absent, for example, urchins multiplied and grazed the forests down to the rock.

[3] The otters' absence from some islands had a human cause. For more than a century, fur traders had hunted the animals for their pelts, that carry the densest fur of any mammal, about a million hairs in a single square inch. By 1911, when an international treaty finally banned the hunt, only a few small colonies survived. Some islands had been recolonized by the time Estes arrived; others had not.

[4] Estes's idea (an animal at the top of a food chain can shape the plants at it's bottom) is now called a trophic cascade. In the 1990s, it received a routine test. Otter numbers across the Aleutians suddenly crashed, and within a few years urchins had stripped many forests bare. Estes and his colleagues suspected killer whales, which may have begun hunting otters after their usual prey grew scarce.

[5] The story shows how much can depend on a single species. An otter weighs about as much as a large dog, but by eating urchins it protects an entire forest and every creature that lives there.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "Around some islands, forests of kelp rises from the rocks, their golden fronds reaching the surface and sheltering schools of fish." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "rises"?
explanation: The subject is "forests," which is plural; "of kelp" only describes it. The verb must be plural and in the present tense, like "lie" and "is" elsewhere in the paragraph: "rise." "Rises" and "is rising" are singular, and "rose" shifts to the past.

passage:
[1] On the night of January 31, 1953, a storm drove the North Sea against the southwestern coast of the Netherlands. The wind arrived together with a spring tide, and the water rose higher than anyone living had seen. Before dawn, the sea had broken through the dikes in dozens of places. By the time it retreated, 1,836 people had drowned, and tens of thousands had lost their homes.

[2] The disaster did not come as a complete surprise. For years an engineer named Johan van Veen had warned that many dikes were to low and too weak. He had even sketched a solution: instead of raising hundreds of miles of dikes, the country could close off the sea arms of the southwestern delta with a few enormous dams, shortening the coastline that had to be defended. Before 1953, his plan seemed too expensive, within three weeks of the flood, the government had formed a commission to carry it out.

[3] The work, called the Delta Works, took more than forty years. The most famous structure, the Eastern Scheldt barrier, was originally meant to be a solid dam. But fishermen and environmentalists objected. A solid dam would turn the estuary behind it into a still lake and destroy the oyster and mussel beds that depended from the tides. After years of debate, engineers designed something new: a barrier of sixty-two steel gates, left open in normal weather and lowered only when a storm threatens. Finished in 1986, it cost far more than a dam but allowed the tides to keep flowing.

[4] The last major piece, a barrier on the waterway leading to Rotterdam was completed in 1997. Its two hinged arms, each nearly as long as the Eiffel Tower is tall, rests in dry docks on the banks. They swing out to close the channel only when the water is forecast to rise dangerously.

[5] Today engineers from other low-lying countries visit the delta to study these structures.
prompt: In paragraph 2, in the sentence "Before 1953, his plan seemed too expensive, within three weeks of the flood, the government had formed a commission to carry it out." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "expensive, within"?
explanation: "Before 1953, his plan seemed too expensive" and "within three weeks of the flood, the government had formed a commission" are independent clauses joined only by a comma, a comma splice. A semicolon joins them. "So" makes the high cost the reason for forming the commission, which is backward, and no punctuation fuses the clauses.

passage:
[1] High in the bell tower of St. Rumbold's Cathedral in Mechelen, Belgium, a musician sits at an instrument that looks like a cross between an organ and a loom. Instead of keys, it has two rows of wooden handles called batons, and a set of pedals below. The musician plays by striking the batons with loosely closed fists. Each baton is connected by a wire to a clapper inside one of the bronze bells hanging overhead, and the sound carries across the whole city.

[2] This instrument is a carillon, and it must have at least twenty-three bells. Carillons first appeared in the towns of Flanders and the Netherlands more than five hundred years ago. In the end, town bells were used to mark the hours, and a few notes were played before the hour struck to warn people to listen. Over time the tunes grew longer, and towns added more bells to play them.

[3] Bells are difficult to tune. A bell sounds not one pitch but several at once, and if those pitches clash, a melody played on it will sound sour. In the 1600s two brothers, François and Pieter Hemony, have learned to shave metal from the inside of a bell on a lathe until its pitches agreed. Their bells were so fragile that many still hang in Dutch towers today.

[4] The carillon owes much of its modern revival to Mechelen. Around 1900 the city's carillonneur, Jef Denyn, improved the mechanism so that a player could control how softly or loudly each bell sounded. His evening concerts drew crowds of thousands into the square below the tower. In 1922 he founded the world's first school for carillon players, and students still travel there from around the world.

[5] Playing a carillon has minor challenges. Each baton, the player must remember, pulls a wire attached to a clapper. The musician sits in a small cabin directly below the bells, where the sound is so loud, and so oddly balanced, that it is hard to judge what listeners on the ground are hearing. And unlike a piano, a carillon has no way to silence a note. Once struck, a large bell may ring for half a minute, every note a player strikes stays in the air long after the next has begun.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "Instead of keys, it has two rows of wooden handles called batons, and a set of pedals below." which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "handles called batons, and"?
explanation: "Called batons" gives the handles' name as an aside, so it is set off by a pair of commas, and the closing comma also separates it from "and a set of pedals." Without the opening comma, the comma before "and" splits two objects of "has"; with only the opening comma, the phrase runs into the next item; and a comma after "called" separates the verb from its complement.

passage:
[1] In the early 1750s, a young tobacco farmer in Maryland borrowed a pocket watch and took it apart. Benjamin Banneker had never seen a clock up close, but he studied the watch's gears until he understood how they worked. Then, using a pocketknife, larger versions of each gear were carved out of wood. The striking clock he built kept time for the rest of his life.

[2] Banneker's clock made him famous throughout Maryland. His grandmother taught him to read from a Bible, and he attended a small country school for a few winters. In contrast, he taught himself, borrowing books whenever he could. He was especially drawn to mathematics, and he liked to solve the puzzles that travelers brought him.

[3] When Banneker was nearly sixty, a neighbor named George Ellicott lent him several books on astronomy and a telescope. Banneker sat up nights in an orchard watching the stars within a year he could predict eclipses. In 1791 George's cousin Andrew Ellicott, a surveyor hired him to help lay out the boundaries of the new federal capital. For three months Banneker kept the expedition's astronomical clock and recorded the positions of stars, from which the surveyors fixed their location.

[4] That same year Banneker completed an almanac, a yearly book of: tide tables, weather predictions, and the times of sunrise and sunset. He mailed the handwritten pages to Thomas Jefferson, then the secretary of state, with a long letter. Jefferson had written that Black people were less capable than white people. Banneker's letter politely reminded him of the words he had written in the Declaration of Independence, that all men are created equal, and offered the almanac as evidence against his opinion.

[5] Jefferson replied within weeks and forwarded the almanac to a scientific academy in Paris. Banneker published his almanacs every year until 1797, and it sold in several states.
prompt: In paragraph 3, in the sentence "Banneker sat up nights in an orchard watching the stars within a year he could predict eclipses." which choice makes the sentence most grammatically acceptable in place of "stars within"?
explanation: Two independent clauses run together with no punctuation. A comma with "and" joins them. A comma alone is a comma splice, and a semicolon followed by "and," with a comma after it, misplaces the pause.

passage:
[1] I signed up for the glassblowing class because the brochure showed a row of glowing vases and I doubted I would make one by the end of the first night. Esperanza Ruelas, who ran the studio out of an old garage on the edge of town had other plans. She handed each of us a steel pipe as long as a broom handle and told us we would spend the evening learning to turn it.

[2] Turning, it turned out, was everything. Molten glass is about as thick as honey, and the moment you stop rotating the pipe, gravity starts pulling the gather toward the floor. [A] For two hours we roll empty pipes back and forth along the arms of a metal bench. [B] My wrists ached by nine o'clock. [C] Esperanza walked behind us, saying nothing except, now and then, "Slower." [D] By the end I could keep a pipe spinning without thinking about it.

[3] The second week we finally worked with real glass. Esperanza dipped the end of my pipe into the furnace and drew out a glowing ball no bigger than a plum. I rolled it on a steel table to shape it, reheated it, and blew a short puff of air into the pipe. The ball shrank slightly and wobbled. Then it slid off the end onto the concrete floor, where it laid glowing like a dropped coal.

[4] I expected her to be annoyed. Instead, she knelt, looked at the blob for a moment, and said that I had stopped turning to watch the bubble grow. She was right, I had been so pleased with myself that I had forgotten the one thing I had practiced for two hours.

[5] By the end of the course I had made six lopsided cups and one small bowl that almost sat flat. The bowl holds paper clips on my desk now. Whenever I look at it, I can still feel the weight of the pipe turning in my hands.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "I signed up for the glassblowing class because the brochure showed a row of glowing vases and I doubted I would make one by the end of the first night." which choice best fits the context of the paragraph in place of "doubted"?
explanation: The narrator signed up "because" of the brochure's vases, and the next sentence says the instructor "had other plans," so the narrator must have expected to make a vase quickly. "Assumed" says that. Doubting would not be a reason to sign up, and the narrator could not regret or forget making something that had not happened yet.

passage:
[1] Every school morning, thousands of teenagers in our district stand at bus stops in the dark, many of them half asleep. The first bell at our high school rings at 7:25, which means many students wake before six. Most of them are not getting enough sleep, and the reason is not, as adults like to assume that they stay up too late on their phones.

[2] Around puberty, the body's internal clock shifts. The hormone that makes people drowsy begin to be released about two hours later in the evening than it was in childhood, so a typical sixteen-year-old cannot easily fall asleep before eleven. Teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. A student who falls asleep at eleven and wakes at six gets seven at most. No amount of discipline at bedtime can close that gap.

[3] When schools have moved their start times later, the results have been striking. However, in 2016 Seattle pushed its high schools' first bell from 7:50 to 8:45. Researchers whom tracked students there found that they slept about half an hour longer on school nights, and their grades in one biology course rose. Attendance improved as well. The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended since 2014 that middle and high schools start no earlier than 8:30.

[4] Critics raise absurd concerns. Buses would have to be rescheduled, and practices for sports teams would run later into the evening. Both changes would cost money and require planning. These problems are real, but other districts have solved them, often by flipping the schedules so that elementary schools, whose younger students wake early anyway, start first.

[5] The evidence is clear, and every year of delay costs another class of students its sleep. Our school board will vote on a new schedule next month, it should approve an 8:30 start for the high school.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "The first bell at our high school rings at 7:25, which means many students wake before six." which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "7:25, which means"?
explanation: The clause beginning "which means" comments on the whole first clause, so it is nonessential and follows a comma. Without the comma it runs into "7:25," a semicolon cannot introduce a dependent clause, and a period leaves "Which means many students wake before six" as a fragment.

passage:
[1] In 1999 a Japanese mobile phone company asked a young employee named Shigetaka Kurita to solve a problem. The company's new service let customers send short e-mails from their phones but each message was limited to 250 characters. Kurita worried that such brief notes would be easy to forge. A plain "Fine" could sound cheerful or cold, and the screen offered no way to tell which.

[2] His solution was a set of 176 tiny pictures; each drawn on a grid only twelve pixels wide and twelve pixels tall. He took ideas from weather forecasts, which used a sun or a cloud to sum up a day, from the symbols in comic books, and he also borrowed from the Chinese characters used in written Japanese. He called them emoji, from the Japanese words for "picture" and "character." Despite the resemblance, the word has nothing to do with the English word "emotion."

[3] The pictures were an instant hit, and rival companies in Japan soon created their own sets. That success, for instance, caused a new problem. A heart sent from one company's phone might arrive on another's as a blank box or a string of nonsense, because each company coded their pictures differently.

[4] The fix came from the Unicode Consortium, a group that assigns a standard number to every letter and symbol in the world's writing systems so that a letter typed on one computer appears correctly on all the others. In 2010, after several years of debate, the consortium added hundreds of emoji to its standard. Within a few years, phones around the world included an emoji keyboard.

[5] In 2016 the Museum of Modern Art in New York acquired Kurita's original 176 designs for its permanent collection. Next to today's detailed, full-color emoji, they look crude, but every one of the thousands that followed descend from them.
prompt: In paragraph 1, in the sentence "The company's new service let customers send short e-mails from their phones but each message was limited to 250 characters." which choice is correctly punctuated in place of "phones but each"?
explanation: Two independent clauses joined by the coordinating conjunction "but" take a comma before the conjunction. A comma after "but" as well separates the conjunction from its clause, and a semicolon is not used before "but" when it joins two clauses like these.
